<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Let $S,T \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$.
\begin{enumerate}[\upshape (1)]
\item $\dim \mathfrak{g}_T = \dim G_T$.
\item $\dim G_T = \dim G - \dim G\cdot T$. 
\item If $S \cong T$, then $\dim G_S = \dim G_T$.
\item If $S \unlhd T$, then $\dim G_S \geq \dim G_T$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $T \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$ be a tensor. Write $T = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i \otimes M_i$ so that $M_1,\dots,M_n$ are the slices of $T$ in direction $3$. (We can similarly define the slices in direction 1 and 2.) We call $T$ \emph{concise} if all of the following three conditions hold:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[(1)] {$\operatorname{rk} (M_1; \dots ; M_n)=n$}
		\item[(2)] {$\operatorname{rk} \begin{pmatrix}
				M_1\\
				\vdots \\
				M_n
			\end{pmatrix}=n$}
		\item[(3)] {$\dim \operatorname{span} (M_1,\dots,M_n)=n$.}
	\end{itemize}
(Equivalently, conciseness means that all three so-called flattening ranks are maximal.)
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Every tensor is equivalent to a subtensor that is concise.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:padding}
Let $m \geq n$, let $T \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$ be concise, and let $S \in \mathbb{C}^m \otimes \mathbb{C}^m \otimes \mathbb{C}^m$ be obtained from $T$ by padding with zeros. Then one can show that $\dim G_S = \dim G_T + 3m(m-n)$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:scalar}\label{ex:unit}
$T = \mathsf{E}_n \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^n e_i \otimes e_i \otimes e_i \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$. Then $\dim G_T = 2n$. Indeed $G_T$ consists of the triples of diagonal matrices $(\operatorname{diag}(a),\operatorname{diag}(b),\operatorname{diag}(c))$ with $a_ib_ic_i = 1$ for all $i$, extended by the diagonally embedded permutation matrices \cite[Theorem~4.3]{burgisser2015fundamentalinvariantsorbitclosures}. 
 Note that $\mathsf{E}_n$ is a direct sum of $n$ copies of $\mathsf{E}_1$. Generally, $\dim G_{S \oplus T} = \dim G_S + \dim G_T$ if $S$ and~$T$ are concise \cite[Lemma~4.2(i)]{Burgisser1997Degen-6409}.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:matmul}
Let $T = \sum_{i,j,k=1}^m e_{i,j} \otimes e_{j,k} \otimes e_{k,i} \in \mathbb{C}^{m^2} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{m^2} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{m^2}$. Writing $T$ as $\operatorname{tr}(XYZ)$, the group $G_T$ is the image of the homomorphism $\operatorname{GL}_m \times \operatorname{GL}_m \times \operatorname{GL}_m \to \operatorname{GL}_{m^2} \times \operatorname{GL}_{m^2} \times \operatorname{GL}_{m^2}$ sending $(A,B,C)$ to $(X \mapsto AXB^{-1},\ Y \mapsto BYC^{-1},\ Z \mapsto CZA^{-1})$ (sometimes called the ``sandwiching action''), a result of de Groote \cite{MR506377} (see also \cite[Theorem~4.5]{burgisser2015fundamentalinvariantsorbitclosures}). Its kernel is $\{(\lambda I, \lambda I, \lambda I) : \lambda \in \mathbb{C}^*\}$, so $\dim G_T = 3m^2-1$ \cite[Lemma~4.2(ii)]{Burgisser1997Degen-6409}.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:null-algebra}
$T = \mathsf{N}_n \coloneqq e_1 \otimes e_1 \otimes e_1 + \sum_{i=2}^n (e_i \otimes e_i \otimes e_1 + e_i \otimes e_1 \otimes e_i) \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$. Then $\dim G_T = n^2+1$, which follows from an explicit Lie algebra computation \cite[Proposition~3.2]{conner2021tensorsmaximalsymmetries}.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:skew}
	Let
    $T = \mathsf{D} \coloneqq e_1 \wedge e_2 \wedge e_3 = \sum_{\pi \in S_3} \operatorname{sign}(\pi)\, e_{\pi(1)} \otimes e_{\pi(2)} \otimes e_{\pi(3)} \in \mathbb{C}^3 \otimes \mathbb{C}^3 \otimes \mathbb{C}^3.$
    Then $G_T$ contains $\{(\lambda g, \mu g, \nu g) : g \in \operatorname{SL}_3, \ \lambda \mu \nu = 1\}$, which has dimension $8 + 2 = 10$, and in fact  $\dim G_T = 10$ (e.g., \cite[Table~3]{MR1773770}, \cite[Remark~3.4]{conner2021tensorsmaximalsymmetries}, \cite[\S7.1]{MR4644081}).
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{th:CGLV}
Let $T \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$ be concise and binding. Then $\dim G_T \leq n^2 + 1$. Equality holds exactly when $T \cong \mathsf{N}_n$ or a permutation of it.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{th:main}
Let $T \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$ be concise. Then $\dim G_T \leq n^2 + 1$. Equality holds exactly when
\begin{enumerate}[\upshape (1)]
\item $T \cong \mathsf{N}_n$ or a permutation of it, or
\item $T \cong \mathsf{D} \coloneqq e_1 \wedge e_2 \wedge e_3 \in \mathbb{C}^3 \otimes \mathbb{C}^3 \otimes \mathbb{C}^3$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{th:matrix-tuple}
Let $M_1, \ldots, M_d \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^d \operatorname{col} M_i = \sum_{i=1}^d \operatorname{row} M_i = \mathbb{C}^n$. Suppose $q < n$, the profiles $r_1, \ldots, r_d$ and $c_1, \ldots, c_d$ are non-increasing, and $r_1 = c_1 = q$. Then
\[
\dim G_{M_1, \ldots, M_d} \leq \sum_{i=1}^d r_i c_i - r_2(q-r_2).
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounded-rank-one}
	Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ be a subspace of matrices all of which have rank $\leq1$. Then, up to equivalence,
	\[
	V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{1,0} \quad\text{or}\quad V\subseteq\mathsf{Comp}_{0,1}.
	\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:max-rank-at-least-2}
	Let $T \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$ concise, $n\geq 2$. Then $\operatorname{Q}_1(T), \operatorname{Q}_2(T), \operatorname{Q}_3(T) \geq 2$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $V$ be the slice span of $T$ in some direction $i$. If $\operatorname{Q}_i(T) \leq 1$, then by \cref{lem:bounded-rank-one}, up to equivalence, $V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{1,0}$ or $V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{0,1}$. Then we see that $T$ is not concise.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounded-rank-two}
	Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$ be a subspace of matrices all of which have rank $\leq 2$. Then, up to equivalence,
	\[
	V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{2,0} \quad\text{or}\quad V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{0,2} \quad\text{or}\quad V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{1,1} \quad\text{or}\quad V = \mathsf{Skew}.
	\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:max-rank-equals-2}
	Let $T \in \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$ concise, $n \geq 3$. Suppose $\operatorname{Q}_3(T) = 2$. Then either
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\operatorname{Q}_1(T) = \operatorname{Q}_2(T) = n$ (binding in direction 1 and 2)
		\item or $T \cong \mathsf{D}$.
	\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $V$ be the slice span of $T$ (in direction $3$). We apply \cref{lem:bounded-rank-two}. Conciseness and $n\geq 3$ rules out $V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{2,0}$ and $V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{0,2}$.
    
    In the case $V \subseteq \mathsf{Comp}_{1,1}$, we can see that $\operatorname{Q}_1(T) = \operatorname{Q}_2(T) = n$. Indeed, let $M_1, \dots, M_n$ be the slices of $T$ in direction $3$, and let $v_{i,j}$ be the $j$-th column of slice $M_i$. Note that $v_{i,j} \in \operatorname{span} (e_1)$ for all $j>1$. Assume $\operatorname{Q}_2(T)<n$, then $\dim \operatorname{span}(v_{1,1},\dots,v_{n,1})<n$. By conciseness of $T$, we know that $\dim \operatorname{span}(v_{i,j}: i,j \in [n])=n$. This forces $\operatorname{Q}_2(T)=n-1$. After appropriate base change, we have $v_{i,1}=e_i$ for all $i>1$, and there exists a $j>1$ such that $v_{1,j}=e_1$. Adding the $j$-th column simultaneously on all slices to the first column yields an isomorphic tensor $T'$ with $\operatorname{Q}_2(T')=n$ which is a contradiction. Hence $\operatorname{Q}_1(T)=\operatorname{Q}_2(T)=n$. 
    
    In the case $V = \mathsf{Skew}$, one can prove that $T \cong \mathsf{D}$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{th:stab-dim-max-rank}
Suppose $q < n$. Then $\dim G_T \leq n^2 + 1 - (q-2)(n-q)$.\footnote{In fact, this statement holds without the assumption $q < n$.}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:n-squared}
	If $2 < q < n$, then $\dim G_T \leq n^2$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
To prove: $\dim G_T \leq n^2 + 1$ and the extremizers are $\mathsf{N}_n$ (and permutations) and $\mathsf{D}$.

Suppose $n=1$, then $T \cong e_1 \otimes e_1 \otimes e_1$ and $\dim G_T = 2 = n^2 + 1$ by \cref{ex:scalar}.

Suppose $n \geq 2$. Suppose $T$ is binding. Then by \cref{th:CGLV} we know that $\dim G_T \leq n^2 + 1$ and that the extremizers are $\mathsf{N}_n$ and permutations.

Suppose $T$ is not binding. Then there is a max-rank $q < n$. We do some basic dimension bookkeeping: By \cref{lem:max-rank-at-least-2}, $q \geq 2$, so $n \geq 3$. We consider two cases for $q$:
 
If $q = 2$, then by \cref{lem:max-rank-equals-2}, either $T$ is binding (which we assumed not) or $T \cong \mathsf{D}$, and $\dim G_T = 10 = n^2 + 1$ by \cref{ex:skew}.
 
If $q \geq 3$, then $\dim G_T \leq n^2$ by \cref{cor:n-squared}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lemma: existance of good basis}
	There is a good basis for $T$ such that
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $c_1 \geq c_2 \geq \cdots \geq c_n$ and $r_1 \geq r_2 \geq \cdots \geq r_n$ and
		\item $c_1 = r_1 = \operatorname{Q}_3(T)$
	\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{M}$ denote the slice span of $T$ in direction 3.
We will construct a basis for $\mathcal{M}$, one slice at a time. Suppose that $M_1, \ldots, M_{k-1}$ have been chosen, and write $W_{k-1} \coloneqq \operatorname{span} \{M_1, \ldots, M_{k-1}\}$. For $M \in \mathcal{M}$, let 
\[
c(M) \coloneqq \dim(U_{k-1} + \operatorname{col} M) - \dim U_{k-1}, \quad r(M) \coloneqq \dim (V_{k-1} + \operatorname{row} M) - \dim V_{k-1}.
\]
We claim that we can choose $M_k \not\in W_{k-1}$ such that $c(M_k)$ and $r(M_k)$ are simultaneously maximised.

Choose a matrix $M$ maximising $c(M)$. Concatenate the columns of $M$ to a fixed basis of $U_{k-1}$ and choose a largest nonzero minor. This minor is a polynomial $f(M)$, nonzero because it does not vanish at the chosen $M$. For any $M' \in \mathcal{M}\setminus W_{k-1}$, if $f(M')\neq 0$, then $c(M') = c(M)$. A nonzero polynomial $g$ detects the maximal value of $r$ in the same way. Finally, since $W_{k-1}$ is a proper subspace of $\mathcal{M}$, some nonzero linear polynomial $h$ vanishes on it. The product $fgh$ is a nonzero polynomial on the complex vector space $\mathcal{M}$, so it is nonzero at some $M_k$. This matrix lies outside $W_{k-1}$ and simultaneously maximises $c(M_k)$ and $r(M_k)$. Repeating the construction gives an ordered basis $M_1, \ldots, M_k$.

At the first step, $U_0 = V_0 = 0$, so the $c(M)$ and $r(M)$ being maximised are both simply $\operatorname{rank}(M)$. Therefore, $c_1 = r_1 = \operatorname{Q}_3(T)$. 

It remains to prove that the two profiles are nonincreasing. Suppose, for instance, that $c_i < c_{i+1}$. At stage $i$, the later slice $M_{i+1}$ was an admissible choise, and its new column constribution relative to $U_{i-1}$ is at least its contribution relative to the larger space $U_i$:
\[
\dim(U_{i-1} + \operatorname{col} M_{i+1}) - \dim U_{i-1} \geq \dim (U_i + \operatorname{col} M_{i+1}) - \dim U_i = c_{i+1} > c_i.
\]
This contradicts the choise of $M_i$. Hence $c_1\geq \cdots \geq c_n$. The same argument with rows gives $r_1 \geq \cdots \geq r_n$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{th:dim-stab-good-basis}
Let $T$ be in a good basis. Suppose $q < n$. Let $d \in [n]$ be the largest such that $c_d > 0$ or $r_d > 0$. Then $\dim G_T \leq nd + \sum_{i=1}^n r_i c_i - (q-1)$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:aux}
$d \leq n-q + 1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n r_i c_i \leq n + q(n-d)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Without loss of generality, $d = \ell(r) \geq \ell(c)$. Then $r_1, \ldots, r_d \geq 1$ and $r_i = c_i = 0$ for $i > d$. Then $d-1 \leq r_2 + \cdots + r_d = n-q$ gives the first claim. For the second, we have
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^n r_i c_i = q^2 + \sum_{i=2}^d c_i + \sum_{i=2}^d (r_i - 1)c_i.
	\]
	We use $\sum_{i=2}^d c_i = n-q$ and $\sum_{i=2}^d (r_i - 1)c_i \leq (n-q-d+1)q$ (since $c_i \leq q$ for all $i$), to get
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^n r_i c_i \leq q^2 + n-q + (n-q-d+1)q = n+q(n-d).\qedhere
	\]
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
We use \cref{th:dim-stab-good-basis} and then the two items from \cref{lem:aux} to get
	\begin{align*}
		\dim G_T &\leq nd + \sum_{i=1}^n r_i c_i - (q-1) \\
		&\leq nd + n + q(n-d) - (q-1) \\
		&= n + qn - (q-1) + (n-q)d \\
		&\leq n + qn - (q-1) + (n-q)(n-q+1)\\
		&= n^2 + 1 - (q-2)(n-q).\qedhere
	\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Recall that $\dim G_T = \dim \mathfrak{g}_T$  
where
\[
\mathfrak{g}_T \coloneq \{(X,Y,Z) : (X \otimes I \otimes I + I \otimes Y \otimes I + I \otimes I \otimes Z)\cdot T = 0\}
\]
which, in terms of the slices $M_1,\ldots, M_n$ of $T$ in direction 3, we can write as
\[
\mathfrak{g}_T = \{(X,Y,Z) : \forall i \in [n], X M_i + M_i Y^T + \sum_{j=1}^n Z_{ij}M_j = 0\}.
\]
Let $\pi : \mathfrak{g}_T \to \mathbb{C}^{d\times n}$ map $(X,Y,Z)$ to the matrix consisting of the first $d$ rows of $Z$. Let $H \coloneqq \{(X,Y) : \forall i \in [d], XM_i + M_i Y^T = 0\}$. We see that if $(X,Y,Z) \in \ker \pi$, then $(X,Y) \in H$. We can also check that $\ker \pi \to H : (X,Y,Z) \mapsto (X,Y)$ is injective. [Indeed, $(X,Y)=0$ implies $\sum_{j=1}^n Z_{ij} M_j=0$ for all $i\in [n]$ and by conciseness of $T$, this implies $Z=0$.] Thus,
\[
\dim \mathfrak{g}_T = \dim \operatorname{im} \pi + \dim \ker \pi \leq nd + \dim H.
\]
It remains to prove $\dim H \leq \sum_{i=1}^n r_i c_i - (q-1)$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Recall we defined the spaces
$U_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^k \operatorname{col} M_i, 
V_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^k \operatorname{row} M_i$ and $c_k \coloneqq \dim U_k - \dim U_{k-1},  r_k \coloneqq \dim V_k - \dim V_{k-1}$. The definition of $d$ as largest index such that $c_d > 0$ or $r_d > 0$, gives $U_d = U_n = \mathbb{C}^n$ and $V_d = V_n = \mathbb{C}^n$. We define
\[
F_k \coloneqq \{(X,Y) \in H : X U_k = 0\}.
\]
We see that
\[
H = F_0 \supseteq F_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq F_d = \dots= F_n= 0.
\]
To see $F_d = 0$: Let $(X,Y) \in F_d$. From $U_d = \mathbb{C}^n$ we get $X = 0$. Then by definition of $H$, $\forall i \in [d], M_iY^T = 0$. Using $V_d = \mathbb{C}^n$ we find $Y^T = 0$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
In the following two claims, we prove an upper bound on  $\dim \operatorname{im} \theta_k$ for all $k$, and a stronger one for $k=0$.
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
\label{claim:1}
	$\forall k, \dim \operatorname{im} \theta_k \leq r_{k+1} c_{k+1}$.
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let
\[
P_k \coloneqq \{ v \in \mathbb{C}^n : M_{k+1} v \in U_k\},\quad Q_k \coloneqq \{w \in (\mathbb{C}^n)^* : w M_{k+1} \in V_k\}.
\]
Then $\operatorname{codim} P_k = c_{k+1}$ and $\operatorname{codim} Q_k = r_{k+1}$.
Let $N \in \operatorname{im} \theta_k$. One readily checks that $N P_k = 0$, and $Q_k N = 0$: there is $(X,Y) \in F_k$ with $N=XM_{k+1}$, then $NP_k=0$ follows directly. Since $(X,Y) \in H$, we observe that for $k+1 \leq d$, we have $N=XM_{k+1}=-M_{k+1}Y^T$ and for $k+1 >d$, we have $F_k=0$ and hence $N=0$. Both imply $Q_kN=0$. This implies that $\operatorname{im} \theta_k$, after appropriate basis transformation, is only supported on an $r_{k+1} \times c_{k+1}$ submatrix, and the dimension bound follows.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- claim-2: body_md -->
\label{claim:2}
	$\dim \operatorname{im} \theta_0 \leq q^2 - (q-1)$.
<!-- end claim-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
After appropriate basis transformation, we have
\[
M_1 = 
\begin{pmatrix}
I_q & 0 \\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix},\,
M_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
M_2^{1,1} & M_2^{1,2}\\
M_2^{2,1} & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
where $M_2^{1,2}$ has rank $r_2$ and $M_2^{2,1}$ has rank $c_2$. Note that from this it follows that $q \geq \operatorname{rank} M_2 \geq r_2 + c_2$. From $q<n$ we get $r_2, c_2 \geq 1$ and so $1 \leq r_2 \leq q-1$, which we will need later. Using $XM_1 + M_1 Y^T = 0$ we find that 
\[
\theta_0(X,Y) = XM_1 = \begin{pmatrix}
	P & 0\\
	0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
for a $q\times q$ matrix $P$. One can then prove that $P( \operatorname{im} M_2^{12} ) \subseteq \operatorname{im} M_2^{12}$ using $XM_2+M_2Y^T=0$. For a fixed $s$-dimensional subspace $S \subseteq \mathbb{C}^q$, the matrices $P \in \mathbb{C}^{q \times q}$ satisfying $P(S) \subseteq S$ form a linear subspace of dimension $q^2 - s(q-s)$. Applying this to our setting with $s = r_2$, gives
\[
\dim \operatorname{im} \theta_0 \leq q^2 - r_2(q-r_2)
\]
Now to see $q^2 - r_2(q-r_2) \leq q^2 - (q-1)$ we use $1 \leq r_2 \leq q-1$ which we established earlier.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
